_about: THE TWO LAYERS MEASURE DIFFERENT THINGS, and this field is the first where
that bites. The US scheme splits employee from self-employed and never asks
hours; the UK scheme splits full-time from part-time and never asks about
self-employment. Those are orthogonal dimensions, not a coarse and a fine
version of one dimension — neither side can produce the other's distinction.
So, as for social_grade, the canonical keeps BOTH and labels what is missing.
'Employed (hours not distinguished)' is where the US layer's employees land; it
is a real value in its own right, not a stand-in for full-time. Mapping it to
full-time would invent an answer; collapsing the UK's hours into it would throw
away a distinction 99,768 rows actually carry.
Two values each layer can never produce, which is correct rather than a gap:
the UK studies never ask about self-employment or disability, and the US studies
have no student category at all. A US student is somewhere inside 'Working - as
a paid employee' or 'Not working - other', so the absence of 'Full time student'
from US rows must NOT be read as the absence of students.
ONE JUDGEMENT, flagged because it is inference rather than transcription. The
8-value YouGov scheme offers bare 'Unemployed' alongside 'Not working', and does
not say which means actively seeking. LOGVPZ's 9-value variant of the same
YouGov family spells it out — 'Unemployed and looking for work' beside 'Not in
paid work for any other reason' — so the bare pair is read the same way. If that
reading is wrong, 'Unemployed' and 'Not working' swap, affecting both.
